lines.text: So, how big is the Earth? Over two thousand years ago, one guy measured it. With a stick.
It's around two hundred forty B.C. in Alexandria, Egypt, and Eratosthenes runs the greatest library on Earth.
He's good at so much that people nickname him Beta. As in: second best at everything.
He hears that down south in [Syene](/sIˈini/), at noon on the longest day of the year, the sun shines straight down a well. No shadows.
But back in Alexandria, same day, same noon, a stick in the ground does cast a shadow. About seven degrees.
The sun is so far away that its rays arrive basically parallel. So on a flat Earth, both shadows would match. They don't. The ground curves.
Seven degrees is about one fiftieth of a circle, so [Syene](/sIˈini/) to Alexandria is one fiftieth of the way around the planet.
How far is that? About five thousand stadia, according to the people who walked it. Ancient GPS was just a guy. Walking. For weeks.
Fifty times five thousand: two hundred fifty thousand stadia around.
Depending on how long a stadion was, that's somewhere between pretty close and almost dead on. The real answer? About forty thousand kilometres.
All with a stick, a well, and some very sore feet. Thanks, Daydream!
So next time somebody calls you second best, remember: Beta measured the planet.
